title: Why Ships Waited Forty Days Before Entering Venice
topic: Why ships waited forty days before entering Venice and Ragusa (the origin of quarantine)

lines: A captain kept his ship anchored offshore, desperate to reach the city.
Venice was close, but his crew could not step ashore.
Between 1348 and 1359, the Black Death wiped out an estimated 30% of Europe's population.
Venice's trade depended on fleets of three thousand three hundred ships.
In 1377, Ragusa made every newcomer wait thirty days on nearby islands.
The captain watched for signs of the plague before anyone could land.
In 1448, the Venetian Senate stretched that wait to forty days.
Dubrovnik built the Lazzarettos, Europe's first quarantine sites.
The word for that wait was quarantena: forty days.
You see, the wait was like waiting out a cough before hugging your family.
Current estimates put the bubonic plague at thirty-seven days from infection to death.
Forty days outlasted the sickness, so the quarantine worked.
Scholars also linked the forty days to Hippocrates, Lent, and alchemy's philosophical month.
Venice gave the world the word quarantine.
But Ragusa began the practice first, with thirty days.

claims.claim: In 1377, newcomers to the city-state of Ragusa had to spend thirty days in a restricted place, originally nearby islands, to see whether Black Death symptoms developed.
In 1448 the Venetian Senate prolonged the waiting period to forty days, giving birth to the term "quarantine" from the Venetian quarantena, meaning forty days.
Current estimates put the bubonic plague's period from infection to death at thirty-seven days, making European forty-day quarantines highly successful at determining crew health.
Dubrovnik was the first city in Europe to set up quarantine sites, the Lazzarettos of Dubrovnik, where arriving ship personnel were held for up to forty days.
Between 1348 and 1359, the Black Death wiped out an estimated 30% of Europe's population, leading governments to establish containment measures.
At the peak of its power and wealth, Venice had 36,000 sailors operating 3,300 ships, dominating Mediterranean commerce.
The original forty-day period was associated with the medical theory of Hippocrates, the Lenten Season of the Christian tradition, and the philosophical month in ancient western alchemy.
